{"rule": "Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and a new passage of about 250 words in the text field.", "text": "The last train through Vellmar ran the winter Margit turned sixty-eight, and the railway sent a man to unscrew the station clock the same week the doctor told her the tremor in her hands would not be going back. She stood on the platform while he worked the brass screws loose, the final punched ticket from December still tucked in her glove, and for a long while the two losses sat side by side in her: the timetable that would now be history and the steady fingers that had already become one.

She went to the platform anyway. Forty years of opening the waiting room at six had laid a groove in her that her feet still found, and the rails did not object to an old woman sweeping snow from a bench no one would sit on. The lamp still hung over the door, the mail hook still jutted from the wall, and when the grey came up over the fields she found herself chalking the temperature on the little board by the office, as if a conductor might lean out and ask.

The village took the bus to Kassel now and said it was quicker. She knew that. She still lifted her flag when a freight rumbled through without stopping, the way she had waved the local in, and once a driver sounded two short notes back, which might have been habit on his side too.

What surprised her was how little the mornings needed her. She had thought herself the stationmaster, the one the line depended on. Now she understood she had mostly been its witness. The trains had never needed her to run; they had needed someone to stand beside the track and to say, quietly, that somewhere was still worth going.

She kept the flag."}
